If you think milking a cow is just pulling on teats, you're wrong.
Most people picture a farmer tugging away like a loose tooth.
But that's not how it works at all.
Inside each teat, a sphincter muscle holds the milk back.
Squeezing the teat shut at the top traps milk in the gland.
Then rolling your fingers down pushes that milk out.
It's a trap-and-push motion, not a pull.
The cow's body only releases milk when she feels safe.
Oxytocin triggers let-down, and the sphincter opens.
Machines copy this rhythm: vacuum on, vacuum off.
Pulsating vacuum mimics the calf's natural suckle.
Sixty pulses per minute, forty percent vacuum, sixty percent rest.
That's the secret: rhythm, not force.
